chief_complaint: dark red-brown urine and muscle pain after trauma
hpi_details: A 71-year-old male presents to the clinic with dark red-brown urine and muscle pain after trauma. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: wonders if the dark urine is connected to the fall and being unable to move afterward
concerns: He is worried his legs are permanently damaged and he will lose his independence and be forced into a nursing home.
expectations: He hopes to get an X-ray to check for internal bleeding and a strong muscle rub or pain medication.

investigation_events.title: Emergency rhabdomyolysis and electrolyte assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: STAT muscle injury, kidney function, electrolyte, and urinalysis results are now available. IV fluid resuscitation and treatment of dangerous electrolyte abnormalities should not be delayed.

results.value: Dipstick strongly positive for blood with only rare RBCs on microscopy

clinical_knowledge.topic: Rhabdomyolysis-induced Acute Kidney Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Rhabdomyolysis-induced Acute Kidney Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation, serial monitoring of CK and electrolytes (particularly potassium), and urgent treatment of any dangerous electrolyte derangements, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dark red-brown urine and muscle pain after trauma

Key HPI features: A 71-year-old male presents to the clinic with dark red-brown urine and muscle pain after trauma. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 108/68, HR 102, afebrile. Tender, swollen muscles of both lower extremities at the site of a crush injury; decreased distal pulses on the affected side. Labs: CK 45,000 U/L (markedly elevated), creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (up from an estimated baseline of 1.0 mg/dL), potassium 5.8 mEq/L, urinalysis dipstick strongly positive for blood but only rare RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria), calcium 7.2 mg/dL (low), phosphate 5.8 mg/dL (elevated).
Relevant background/PMH: Unremarkable; found after a fall with several hours of immobilization
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Rhabdomyolysis-induced Acute Kidney Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hemolysis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Muscle weakness or palpitations — hyperkalemia risk.
management_principles: Start aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation immediately, titrated to maintain adequate urine output
Check serial CK, creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, and bicarbonate; treat hyperkalemia urgently given the arrhythmia risk
Involve nephrology early and consider dialysis if refractory hyperkalemia, oliguric AKI, or volume overload develops
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: dark red-brown urine and muscle pain after trauma

A 71-year-old male presents about 12 hours after a fall with prolonged immobilization, with severe bilateral leg pain, swelling, and dark tea-colored urine. Reports minimal oral intake since the fall.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 108/68, HR 102, afebrile. Tender, swollen muscles of both lower extremities at the site of a crush injury; decreased distal pulses on the affected side. Labs: CK 45,000 U/L (markedly elevated), creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (up from an estimated baseline of 1.0 mg/dL), potassium 5.8 mEq/L, urinalysis dipstick strongly positive for blood but only rare RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria), calcium 7.2 mg/dL (low), phosphate 5.8 mg/dL (elevated).
reference_soap.assessment: Rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury following prolonged immobilization after a fall, evidenced by markedly elevated CK, myoglobinuria, rising creatinine, and hyperkalemia.
reference_soap.plan: Start prompt isotonic IV fluid resuscitation with close monitoring of urine output and volume status. Measure serial CK, creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, and bicarbonate, and treat dangerous electrolyte abnormalities. Do not use urine alkalinization routinely; involve nephrology and consider dialysis for standard refractory indications.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Rhabdomyolysis AKI
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Rhabdomyolysis AKI
Implement evidence-based management plan: Aggressive IV hydration with Normal Saline, check CK and urine pH

teaching.one_liner: Muscle injury from trauma releases myoglobin into the bloodstream, which is directly toxic to the kidney tubules, causing dark red-brown urine and elevated CK.
red_flags: Muscle weakness or palpitations — hyperkalemia risk

must_ask.say: What happened — can you describe the injury?
How severe is the muscle pain, and where?
How much have you been drinking since the injury?

history.answer: I had a bad fall at home and now my legs hurt terribly, and when I went to the bathroom my urine was dark red-brown like tea.
The fall happened about twelve hours ago, and since then the leg pain has gotten worse and my urine turned very dark.
It looks dark reddish-brown, almost like black tea or cola. I have not noticed any blood clots in it.
The entire stream was that dark brown color from start to finish.
No, it doesn't burn or hurt when the urine comes out; the terrible pain is in my leg muscles.
No, I don't have any pain in my sides or my groin.
No burning, and I haven't felt a sudden urge or needed to go more often than usual.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweats.
No, the stream seems normal when I go, and I don't feel like urine is left behind.
My legs are very swollen and tight, and I've only urinated once or twice since the fall with very little coming out. My face isn't puffy though.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, skin sores, or any colds recently.
No rashes, joint aches, or coughing up blood.
I haven't lost weight, but I feel completely exhausted and drained since the fall.
No nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or abnormal bruising anywhere else.
No, I don't take aspirin, warfarin, or any other blood-thinning pills.
I tripped over a rug at home about twelve hours ago and couldn't get up for several hours because my legs were pinned. I haven't done any heavy workouts.
No, I haven't eaten beets, berries, or taken any new medications or vitamins.
No, I have never had kidney stones or kidney problems in the past.
I'm retired from an office job and haven't handled dyes, rubber, or toxic chemicals.
Both of my thighs and calves ache severely and feel rock-hard and swollen, especially where I was lying on them.
I haven't had anything to drink since the fall because I couldn't reach any water while stuck on the floor.
My heart has been beating a bit fast, but I don't have chest pain, fluttering, or trouble breathing.
My legs ache so badly I can't even stand, and I'm terrified I won't be able to live on my own anymore and will end up in a nursing home.
I've been generally healthy with no high blood pressure, diabetes, or chronic medical conditions.
I had an appendectomy when I was a young man, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I don't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter pills, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have an occasional glass of beer or wine when socializing, nothing heavy.
I am a retired accountant and I live alone in an apartment.
There is no family history of kidney failure, dialysis, or bleeding disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Elderly male lying supine in moderate distress from lower extremity pain, alert and oriented with dry oral mucosa.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, without palpable masses or suprapubic distension.
Bilateral calves and thighs are visibly swollen, tense, and exquisitely tender to light palpation.
Marked bilateral lower extremity swelling without pitting; no periorbital or facial edema.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are diminished bilaterally; radial pulses are intact.
Contusions and pressure erythema across both lower extremities without petechiae, purpura, or active bleeding.
Normal sphincter tone with smooth, non-tender prostate without discrete nodules.
Upper extremity strength is 5/5 bilaterally; bilateral lower extremity active movement is severely limited by pain to 3/5.
